subject: Vocabulary
description: Latin CRED (believe) and FID (trust, faith) roots — credible, credit, incredible, fidelity, confidence, perfidious, infidel.

options.option_text: Believable, trustworthy, plausible
Untrustworthy, deceitful here
Famous and well-known person
Wealthy and well-connected only

questions.explanation: CREDIBLE — etymology: Latin 'credere' (to believe) + '-ible' (capable of) = 'capable of being believed' = trustworthy, plausible. WORD FAMILY (root CRED = believe): (1) CREDIBLE — believable. (2) INCREDIBLE — UN-believable; extraordinary. (3) CREDIT — trust given (financial/social). (4) DISCREDIT — destroy credibility. (5) CREDITOR — one to whom money is owed (trusted you with debt). (6) CREDIBILITY — quality of being believable. (7) CREDENTIAL — proof/document of identity, authority. (8) ACCREDIT — give official recognition (institutions). (9) CREED — set of beliefs (religious/philosophical). (10) CREDO — Latin for 'I believe'; statement of belief. (11) CREDULOUS — too trusting, easily deceived. (12) INCREDULOUS — disbelieving, skeptical. EXAMPLES: 'A credible witness' = trustworthy; 'Incredible story' = hard to believe; 'Get credit' = receive trust; 'Credentials' = qualifications proving authority; 'Credulous person' = easily fooled. EXAM TRAP: distinguish CREDIBLE (believable) vs CREDULOUS (gullible). 'A CREDIBLE person believes EVIDENCE; a CREDULOUS person believes ANYTHING.' UPSC English: vocab proficiency tested in Mains essay + Indian-language Paper. PYQ FREQUENCY: CRED root in SSC CGL, CAT, IBPS PO English 1-2× per cycle.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: Extraordinary; hard to believe
Easily believable, ordinary
Boring or commonplace items
Forbidden, taboo, illegal

questions.explanation: INCREDIBLE — etymology IN (not) + CREDIBLE (believable) = 'NOT BELIEVABLE'. COMMON USAGE: extraordinary, amazing, beyond normal expectation; sometimes literally 'unbelievable' (questioning truth). EXAMPLES: (1) 'INCREDIBLE INDIA' — Tourism Ministry's marketing campaign (since 2002, by Ministry of Tourism + Ogilvy & Mather agency); designed to attract foreign tourists by showcasing India's diversity, heritage, culture. (2) 'The view from Mt Everest is incredible' = breathtaking. (3) 'Her story sounds incredible' = hard to believe (literal). (4) 'She has incredible talent' = extraordinary. NUANCE — POSITIVE vs SKEPTICAL: 'incredible' often POSITIVE (amazing), but in context of stories/claims = SKEPTICAL (suspicious of truth). 'I find his alibi incredible' (don't believe). DUAL-USE WORDS like INCREDIBLE: meaning depends on context. SYNONYMS for the POSITIVE sense: amazing, awesome, breathtaking, extraordinary, marvellous, phenomenal, remarkable, spectacular, stupendous, unbelievable. SYNONYMS for SKEPTICAL: implausible, dubious, far-fetched, suspicious. RELATED — INCREDULOUS (different word!) — describes the PERSON who doesn't believe; not the THING. 'She gave me an incredulous look' (her expression was disbelieving). CONFUSION: incredible (about a thing) vs incredulous (about a person's response) — common exam trap! PYQ FREQUENCY: incredible/incredulous distinction in SSC CGL, CAT, IBPS PO 1× per cycle.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: Faithfulness, loyalty (e.g., to spouse)
Wealth and prosperity here
Highest social status only
Boldness in difficult situations

questions.explanation: FIDELITY — etymology Latin 'fidelis' (faithful) + '-ity' = 'state of being faithful'. Means LOYALTY, FAITHFULNESS, especially in marriage or to a cause. WORD FAMILY (root FID = trust, faith): (1) FIDELITY — loyalty. (2) INFIDELITY — unfaithfulness (esp. marital). (3) CONFIDENT — having full trust. (4) CONFIDE — trust someone with secrets. (5) CONFIDENTIAL — secret; trusted. (6) DIFFIDENT — lacking confidence (DI = away). (7) FIDUCIARY — based on trust (financial relationship). (8) PERFIDIOUS — treacherous (PER = through/away, in negative sense). (9) INFIDEL — non-believer (in religious context — historically pejorative; modern usage avoids). (10) BONA FIDE — 'in good faith' (Latin); genuine. (11) AFFIDAVIT — sworn statement (legal). DISTINCT MEANINGS — FIDELITY in different contexts: (a) MARITAL — loyalty to spouse. (b) DOG'S FIDELITY — loyalty to owner (proverbial). (c) AUDIO — high-fidelity (HiFi) sound = TRUE-to-original reproduction. (d) HISTORICAL — fidelity to source documents (no distortion). MOTTO usage: many institutions have 'FIDELITY' or related Latin phrases — US Marines: 'Semper Fidelis' (Always Faithful, since 1883). EDINBURGH ROYAL HIGH SCHOOL: 'Musis Respublica Floret' but variants. UPSC angle: Indian Penal Code Section 497 (adultery — struck down 2018 by SC, Joseph Shine v. Union of India; fidelity is moral/social, not criminal). PYQ FREQUENCY: FID root vocab in SSC CGL, CAT 1× per cycle.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: Trust someone with secrets/feelings
Hide everything carefully here
Combine multiple things together
Confine someone in jail or prison

questions.explanation: CONFIDE — etymology Latin 'con' (together with) + 'fidere' (to trust) = 'to share trust together'. Means to TRUST SOMEONE with private info, secrets, deep feelings. SAMPLE: 'She confides in her best friend.' 'The patient confided his fears to his doctor.' RELATED WORDS: (1) CONFIDENCE — state of trusting; self-trust. (2) CONFIDENT — having self-trust. (3) CONFIDENTIAL — secret, trusted. (4) CONFIDANT (m) / CONFIDANTE (f) — close friend trusted with secrets. (5) CONFIDENTIALITY — duty of keeping secrets. (6) DIFFIDENT — opposite of confident; lacking confidence. KEY DISTINCTION: (a) CONFIDE IN — share secrets/feelings (intransitive). 'She confides IN him' = she shares with him. (b) CONFIDE TO — entrust formally (less common). 'He confided his savings to the bank.' EXAM TRAP: don't confuse 'CONFIDE' with: (1) CONFINE — restrict (trap, limit, imprison). 'Confine to bed' = bedridden. Different etymology: 'finis' (end, boundary). (2) CONFOUND — confuse, baffle. (3) CONFUTE — disprove. UPSC angle: CONFIDENTIALITY in governance + journalism (RTI exemptions for confidential matters; legal privileges for lawyer-client communication). 'WHISTLEBLOWER' protections (Whistle Blowers Protection Act 2014). PYQ FREQUENCY: CONFIDE/CONFIDENCE-related vocab in SSC CGL, CAT, IBPS PO 1× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests careful reading + word-association.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: Treacherous; deceitful, betraying trust
Highly faithful, trustworthy person
Strong and physically powerful
Wealthy and influential person

questions.explanation: PERFIDIOUS — etymology Latin 'per' (through, beyond — in negative sense) + 'fid' (trust/faith) = 'breaking through trust' = TREACHEROUS, deceitful, faithless. ANTONYM of FAITHFUL. NOUN: PERFIDY = act of betrayal. SAMPLE: 'A perfidious ally betrayed our plans.' 'The perfidious king broke his oath.' STRONG NEGATIVE word — implies SERIOUS BREACH OF TRUST. SYNONYMS: treacherous, traitorous, deceitful, untrustworthy, two-faced, double-dealing, false. ANTONYMS: faithful, loyal, trustworthy, dependable. KEY 'PER-' MEANINGS: (1) THROUGH (perimeter, perforate). (2) THOROUGHLY (perfect = thoroughly done). (3) NEGATIVE (perjury = lying, perfidious = breaking trust, perish = thoroughly dead). (4) PERMEATE — go through. (5) PERSPECTIVE — through-look. KEY 'FID-' WORDS revisited: PERFIDIOUS contrasts with FIDUCIARY (trust-based duty). 'Perfidious Albion' — historic French slur on Britain (~17-18th century) for diplomatic betrayals. RELATED WORDS: TREACHERY (act of betrayal), TREASON (legally, betrayal of state — punishable under IPC Section 121-124, Indian Constitution defines treason indirectly through these). UPSC angle: 'sedition' (IPC 124A) is a related but distinct concept — recently struck down/restrained by SC (May 2022 stay; ongoing review). KEY: SC observed 124A may not survive constitutional scrutiny. PYQ FREQUENCY: PERFIDIOUS in CAT, GRE, advanced UPSC English 1× per cycle.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: In good faith; genuine, sincere
False, fraudulent, illegitimate
Bored or weary, unenthused
Bonus given to officials only

questions.explanation: BONA FIDE — Latin: 'bona' (good) + 'fide' (faith, ablative of 'fides') = 'in good faith'. Means GENUINE, AUTHENTIC, SINCERE; without intent to deceive. PRONUNCIATION: 'BOH-nah FY-dee' (Latin) or 'bo-NAH FYD' (Anglicized). USAGE: (1) 'A bona fide offer' = genuine. (2) 'Bona fide passenger' = legitimate (traveling for genuine reason). (3) Indian Railways: 'BONA FIDE PASSENGER' = legitimate ticket-holder; differs from ticketless travelers. (4) LEGAL: 'Bona fide purchaser' = buyer who purchased in good faith without knowledge of defects. RELATED LATIN LEGAL phrases: (1) MALA FIDE = 'in bad faith' (opposite). (2) DE FACTO = 'in fact' (in practice). (3) DE JURE = 'in law' (in legal theory). (4) HABEAS CORPUS = 'have the body' (writ to produce a person before court — Article 32, 226 in Indian Constitution). (5) SUO MOTU = 'on its own motion' (court taking action without petition). (6) MUTATIS MUTANDIS = 'with necessary changes'. (7) PRO BONO = 'for good' (free legal services). (8) AMICUS CURIAE = 'friend of the court' (advisor to court). UPSC angle: legal terminology in GS-2 polity; SC judgments use these regularly. CIVIL SERVICE law-officer roles (AG, SG) use these phrases professionally. PYQ FREQUENCY: BONA FIDE + Latin phrases in CAT, UPSC, judicial services 1-2× per cycle.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: Lacks confidence; shy, hesitant
Is highly confident and bold
Is contradictory and conflicting
Has different opinions from others

questions.explanation: DIFFIDENT — etymology DIS (apart, away, away from) + FID (trust) = 'lacking trust (in oneself)' = SHY, RESERVED, HESITANT. ANTONYM of CONFIDENT. SAMPLE: 'The diffident new student didn't speak up.' 'She's diffident about asking for help.' SYNONYMS: shy, reserved, timid, hesitant, self-effacing, unassertive, retiring. ANTONYMS: confident, assertive, self-assured, bold, outspoken. EXAM TRAP: students confuse: (1) DIFFIDENT — lacking confidence. (2) DIFFERENT — not the same. — These are DIFFERENT words despite similar appearance. ETYMOLOGICALLY DIFFERENT roots: 'diffident' (DIS + FID); 'different' (DIS + FERRE — to carry, separate). KEY: 'difficult' is also separate (DIS + FACERE). FAMILY of CONFIDENCE-related words: (1) CONFIDENT (assured) ↔ DIFFIDENT (uncertain). (2) CONFIDENCE ↔ DIFFIDENCE. (3) SELF-CONFIDENT ↔ INSECURE. (4) ASSERTIVE ↔ SUBMISSIVE. (5) BOLD ↔ TIMID. (6) DECISIVE ↔ INDECISIVE. PSYCHOLOGY angle: diffidence = trait or state. State diffidence → in unfamiliar situations (mostly normal); trait diffidence → personality (may benefit from social-skills training, CBT, exposure therapy). UPSC INTERVIEW PERSONALITY: candidates are evaluated on confidence (without arrogance) — diffidence often penalized; ASSERTIVENESS WITH HUMILITY is the gold standard. PYQ FREQUENCY: DIFFIDENT in CAT, GRE, advanced UPSC English 1× per 2 cycles. EXAMINER MINDSET (UPSC-level): tests vocabulary precision.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: A job applicant submits their CREDENTIALS to prove eligibility for a post. Which meaning of CREDENTIALS best fits this context?

options.option_text: Personal opinions shared during a job interview session
Documented evidence of qualifications, skills, or authority
Letters of recommendation from previous employers only
Employment contract outlining salary and job responsibilities

questions.explanation: CREDENTIALS comes from Latin 'credentialis' (CRED = believe), meaning things that entitle belief in one's claims — documents proving qualifications or authority. Option C is wrong because credentials is broader than just recommendation letters; it includes degrees, certificates, and identity proofs.

questions.stem: An AFFIDAVIT is a legal document whose name derives from the Latin FID root (faith/pledge). What is the defining characteristic of an affidavit?

options.option_text: A contract signed by two parties to resolve a financial dispute
An official order issued by a court to compel witness testimony
A sworn written statement confirmed by oath or solemn affirmation
A government-issued certificate confirming identity and residence

questions.explanation: AFFIDAVIT comes from Medieval Latin 'affidavit' meaning 'he has pledged his faith' (FID root). It is a voluntary written statement made under oath, making C correct. Option B (court summons) confuses affidavit with a subpoena — a subpoena compels appearance, whereas an affidavit is a pledged written declaration.

questions.stem: In which sentence is CREDULOUS used CORRECTLY?

options.option_text: Her credulous research methodology impressed the review panel greatly.
He was so credulous that he fell for every online scam he encountered.
The report's credulous findings were published in a scientific journal.
She was the most credulous expert on taxation policy in the country.

questions.explanation: CREDULOUS (CRED = believe) means too willing to believe things without adequate evidence — it describes people, not methods or findings. Option B correctly applies it to a person who naively trusts scams. Options A, C, and D misuse it where CREDIBLE (worthy of belief/trust) would be correct — a very common exam-tested confusion.

questions.stem: A political party's CREDO, directly from Latin CREDO meaning 'I believe', is best described as?

options.option_text: Its foundational declaration of core beliefs and governing values
Its official list of candidates for the upcoming general election
The financial accounts submitted annually to the election commission
The coalition agreement negotiated between allied parties after polls

questions.explanation: CREDO is first-person singular of 'credere' (CRED root = to believe); it means a statement of beliefs or guiding principles. Option A is correct. Option D is a tempting distractor because political parties do negotiate coalition agreements, but that is a pragmatic pact, not a declaration of belief — a credo is ideological, not contractual.

questions.stem: The word INFIDEL combines Latin IN- (not) + FIDELIS (faithful, from FID root). In its classical historical usage, an infidel referred to?

options.option_text: A soldier who abandoned their regiment during active military service
A merchant who deliberately defaulted on trade agreements with partners
A foreign envoy who violated diplomatic protocols during state visits
A person considered to lack faith in a dominant religion of the time

questions.explanation: INFIDEL = IN (not) + FIDELIS (faithful, from FID = faith/trust), literally 'one who is not faithful.' Historically it denoted someone outside the dominant faith — used by both Christian Crusaders and Islamic writers for non-believers. Options A, B, and C describe betrayal of duty or contracts, which confuse the FID root's meaning of religious faith with general loyalty.

questions.stem: MISCREANT traces to Old French 'mescreant' (one who does not believe rightly), sharing the CRED root via Latin 'miscredere'. Today, a MISCREANT most closely denotes?

options.option_text: A deeply devout person who follows religious doctrines very strictly
A chronic wrongdoer who habitually violates moral or legal standards
Someone who questions religious dogma on rational philosophical grounds
A highly gullible individual who accepts falsehoods without any scrutiny

questions.explanation: MISCREANT evolved from 'one who believes wrongly (heretic)' to its modern sense of a habitual criminal or villain, retaining the moral-transgression core of the CRED root. Option C is a trap — questioning religious dogma sounds like the etymological sense of 'wrong belief', but miscreant today has no religious connotation and specifically means a lawbreaker or scoundrel. Option D confuses miscreant with CREDULOUS.

questions.stem: A trustee who prioritises personal gain over a beneficiary's welfare breaches their _____ obligation. Which word correctly fills the blank?

options.option_text: CREDULOUS — describing a person who is naively and excessively trusting
CREDIBLE — meaning capable of being believed due to reliable evidence
FIDUCIARY — denoting a duty to act solely in another's best interest
INFIDEL — denoting one who lacks faith in a religion or belief system

questions.explanation: FIDUCIARY comes from Latin 'fiduciarius' (FID root = trust/faith), meaning a person or duty involving trust — specifically the legal obligation to act in the best interest of another (trustee, guardian, financial adviser). Option A (CREDULOUS) is a strong distractor because trust is involved in both contexts, but CREDULOUS describes a personality trait of over-believing, not a legal duty. FIDUCIARY is the precise legal/financial term tested in IBPS PO and SSC CGL exams.
